paragraphs.heading: A blanket of gas
paragraphs.text: Earth's atmosphere is a layered mix of gases, commonly called air, held around the planet by gravity. Like the atmospheres of other planets, it also carries varying amounts of suspended aerosols and particles that make clouds and haze. It gets thinner with height and has no sharp boundary with space, though the Kármán line at 100 km is often used as a conventional edge. Its total mass is about 5.15×10¹⁸ kg, and three-quarters of that sits within about 11 km of the ground.

paragraphs.heading: What it does for us
paragraphs.text: The atmosphere shields the surface from most meteoroids and from most ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. It narrows the gap between daytime and nighttime temperatures, and it keeps the surface warm by holding in heat through the greenhouse effect. Air currents carry heat and moisture from one region to another. It also supplies the chemical and climate conditions in which life can exist and evolve. Air fit for land plants to photosynthesize and land animals to breathe is found in the troposphere.

paragraphs.heading: What air is made of
paragraphs.text: Counted by molecules, dry air is 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus small amounts of trace gases. Water vapor varies, averaging around 1% at sea level and 0.4% across the whole atmosphere. In the lower atmosphere its share ranges from tiny amounts in the coldest regions up to 5% in hot, humid air masses, and other gases are usually quoted as shares of dry air, without water vapor. The trace gases include other greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone.

paragraphs.heading: An atmosphere that changed
paragraphs.text: Earth's first atmosphere was mostly hydrogen and helium gathered from the solar nebula. Over time it changed through gases escaping to space, volcanism, impacts and weathering. By the Archean eon it had become a second atmosphere dominated by nitrogen and methane. Then cyanobacteria, life forms that use sunlight to split water and give off oxygen, released oxygen so steadily that the atmosphere's chemistry changed for good, in an event called the Great Oxygenation Event. Later rounds of oxygenation produced today's air, dominated by nitrogen and oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: Layers and mixing
paragraphs.text: Scientists divide the atmosphere into layers by traits such as temperature and composition: the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. Up to about 100 km, turbulence stirs the gases so their proportions stay the same. Between roughly 80 and 120 km, that stirring gradually gives way to molecular diffusion. This forms a region called the heterosphere, where lighter gases make up a growing share the higher you go.

paragraphs.heading: The ragged outer edge
paragraphs.text: The exosphere is the outermost layer, so thin that some scientists count it as part of interplanetary space instead. It starts at the exobase, the top of the thermosphere, which sits at about 500 km and rises to about 1,000 km when incoming solar radiation is stronger. Its outer limit is fuzzy: some authorities place it near 10,000 km, others near 190,000 km, about halfway to the Moon. The layer is mostly hydrogen at extremely low density, and its particles sit so widely spaced that each can cover hundreds of kilometres before bumping into another.
